name: Jamaica
summary_text: Jamaica is dangerous for trans visitors. The Offences Against the Person Act (buggery law, up to 10 years) remains on the books and shapes police culture; there is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The defining case is Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed, and shot to death by a mob at a 2013 street party after being outed — whose killing police failed to investigate, now the subject of an Inter-American Commission case (Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica) documenting state failure to protect trans life. Police harassment of trans women is documented in the public-health literature, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people remains a live risk — community members report that violence against trans people (beatings, stonings) is common but rarely reported because there is no point. Tourist resorts (Montego Bay, Negril, Ocho Rios) are heavily insulated bubbles where incidents are rare, but a visibly trans visitor outside them faces real outing-violence risk with indifferent police.

sources.claim_summary: Amicus brief (Feb 2024) to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights in Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica (murder of a trans teenager), presented by TransWave Jamaica and other Caribbean trans organisations with law-school clinics: documents systemic discrimination against LGBTQ people in Jamaica, with transgender people particularly vulnerable to housing insecurity and educational/employment exclusion.
NOTE: The UNDP report 'Being LGBTI in Jamaica' (Nov 2023) returned no extractable text at fetch time (image-based PDF).

sources.claim_summary: PubMed entry: 'Associations between Police Harassment and HIV Vulnerabilities among Men Who Have Sex with Men and Transgender Women in Jamaica' (Health and Human Rights, Dec 2017) — links police harassment of MSM and trans women to HIV vulnerability.

Canadian IRB Response to Information Request (Dec 2010) on how Jamaican police treat complaints by LGBT people (2007-2010): NGOs document police harassment - mostly verbal abuse but also physical abuse; the buggery law (up to 10 years with hard labour) and 'gross indecency' between males (up to 2 years) are used to harass men perceived to be gay.

IACHR (OAS) Report on the Situation of Human Rights in Jamaica (Aug 2012): comprehensive official assessment - citizen security, police killings (including May 2010), administration of justice, police impunity, and the situation of LGBT persons.

sources.title: Letter Urging Jamaican Government to Protect Rights Defenders and Address Violence and Abuse Based on Sexual Orientation and HIV | Human Rights Watch
sources.claim_summary: Human Rights Watch (Nov 2004): letter urging Jamaica's government to protect rights defenders and address violence and abuse based on sexual orientation, after its 'Hated to Death' HIV/homophobia report provoked official denials.

sources.title: GayToday.com - Top Story
sources.claim_summary: GayToday (2006): Amnesty International's urgent appeal on Jamaica - vigilante violence and police torture; gay men and women 'beaten, cut, burned, raped and shot'; a J-FLAG account of a mob beating a man while chanting 'battyman fi' dead'; Amnesty urged repeal of the criminalising law.
